about: LL142 Contract Law is a compulsory one-unit course on the LSE LLB in Laws (also compulsory on the BA in Anthropology and Law). According to the 2026/27 course guide, it covers the general principles of the English common law of contract (formation, interpretation, defences such as misrepresentation and duress, breach and remedies) and asks whether the doctrines are justified given their social consequences. Teaching in 2026/27 is lectures and classes across Autumn and Winter Terms (plus 2 hours of lectures and 1 hour of classes in Spring Term), with two formative written assessments. Assessment is a single 180-minute exam (plus 15 minutes' reading time) in the Spring exam period, worth 100%.
topics: Formation: consideration, promissory estoppel and intention to create legal relations
Interpretation, implied terms and statutory control of terms
Defences: duress and related pressure doctrines
Remedies: specific performance, injunctions, agreed sums and penalties

notes.body:
LL142 opens with formation, and Gibson v Manchester City Council [1979] 1 WLR 294 (HL) is one of the cases the 2026/27 course guide names. Formation questions ask two things: did the parties reach agreement, and is that agreement certain enough to enforce?

The objective test
English law judges agreement objectively: what would a reasonable person in the other party's position have understood the words and conduct to mean? A party's private, uncommunicated intention does not count (Smith v Hughes (1871) LR 6 QB 597).

Offer or invitation to treat?
An offer is a statement of terms by which the maker intends to be bound as soon as the other party accepts. An invitation to treat only invites offers.
- Gibson: a council letter saying it "may be prepared to sell" a house was not an offer, so the tenant's reply could not be an acceptance. Lord Diplock accepted that a few cases do not fit the offer-and-acceptance analysis, but said the ordinary approach applied here.
- Goods on self-service shelves are an invitation to treat; the customer offers at the till (Pharmaceutical Society of Great Britain v Boots Cash Chemists (Southern) Ltd [1953] 1 QB 401).
- Goods in a shop window (Fisher v Bell [1961] 1 QB 394) and most newspaper adverts (Partridge v Crittenden [1968] 1 WLR 1204) are invitations to treat.
- An advert can be a unilateral offer to the world if it shows a clear intention to be bound, as in Carlill v Carbolic Smoke Ball Co [1893] 1 QB 256, where the company's £1,000 bank deposit showed seriousness. Performing the requested act is acceptance and notice of acceptance is waived.

Acceptance
- It must match the offer exactly. A counter-offer rejects the original offer, which cannot later be accepted (Hyde v Wrench (1840) 3 Beav 334). A mere request for information is not a counter-offer (Stevenson, Jacques & Co v McLean (1880) 5 QBD 346).
- Battle of the forms: the traditional analysis usually gives the contract to the "last shot" fired before performance (Butler Machine Tool Co v Ex-Cell-O Corp [1979] 1 WLR 401; reaffirmed in Tekdata Interconnections Ltd v Amphenol Ltd [2009] EWCA Civ 1209).
- Acceptance must normally be communicated; silence is not acceptance (Felthouse v Bindley (1862) 11 CB NS 869).
- Instantaneous communications take effect when and where received (Entores v Miles Far East Corp [1955] 2 QB 327; Brinkibon Ltd v Stahag Stahl [1983] 2 AC 34).
- Postal rule: a properly posted acceptance takes effect on posting (Adams v Lindsell (1818) 1 B & Ald 681), unless the offer excludes it, e.g. by requiring "notice in writing" (Holwell Securities v Hughes [1974] 1 WLR 155).

Revocation
An offer can be withdrawn at any time before acceptance, but revocation takes effect only when communicated (Byrne & Co v Van Tienhoven (1880) 5 CPD 344). It may be communicated by a reliable third party (Dickinson v Dodds (1876) 2 Ch D 463). The postal rule does not apply to revocation.

Certainty and completeness
- Terms that are too vague cannot be enforced: "on hire-purchase terms" in Scammell and Nephew Ltd v Ouston [1941] AC 251.
- Courts try to uphold commercial deals, especially where the parties have acted on them (Hillas & Co v Arcos Ltd (1932) 147 LT 503).
- A bare agreement to negotiate is unenforceable (Walford v Miles [1992] 2 AC 128).
- Where parties start performing before signing, a contract may arise from conduct even if documents were marked "subject to contract", if the parties waived that condition (RTS Flexible Systems Ltd v Molkerei Alois Müller GmbH [2010] UKSC 14).

Social questions the course raises
LL142 asks whether doctrines are justified by their social effects. Ask, for example, whether the objective test protects reasonable reliance, and whether the battle-of-the-forms rule rewards whoever has the better paperwork.

Exam tips: identify each communication in time order and label it (invitation, offer, counter-offer, request for information, acceptance, revocation); then apply the timing rules.

A promise is enforceable in English law if it is given for consideration (or made by deed). Williams v Roffey Bros & Nicholls (Contractors) Ltd [1991] 1 QB 1 (CA) is on the LL142 indicative reading list for 2026/27, so expect the debate about it.

What counts as consideration
- Consideration is the price for which the promise is bought: a benefit to the promisor or a detriment to the promisee (Currie v Misa (1875) LR 10 Ex 153; Dunlop v Selfridge [1915] AC 847).
- It must move from the promisee (Tweddle v Atkinson (1861) 1 B & S 393), although a third party may now enforce a term under the Contracts (Rights of Third Parties) Act 1999, s 1.
- It must be sufficient but need not be adequate: chocolate wrappers in Chappell & Co v Nestlé [1960] AC 87; £1 a year rent in Thomas v Thomas (1842) 2 QB 851.
- Past consideration is no consideration (Re McArdle [1951] Ch 669), unless the act was done at the promisor's request, both understood it would be paid for, and payment would have been enforceable (Pao On v Lau Yiu Long [1980] AC 614, PC, building on Lampleigh v Brathwait (1615)).

Performing an existing duty
- A public duty imposed by law is not consideration (Collins v Godefroy (1831)), but doing more than the duty is (Glasbrook Bros v Glamorgan CC [1925] AC 270).
- A duty already owed to a third party can be good consideration (Scotson v Pegg (1861); The Eurymedon [1975] AC 154).
- A contractual duty already owed to the promisor: Stilk v Myrick (1809) 2 Camp 317 held that it was not consideration. In Williams v Roffey, the Court of Appeal held that a promise to pay more for the same work can be binding where the promisor obtains a practical benefit (e.g. avoiding a late-completion penalty and the trouble of finding a replacement) and the promise was not obtained by economic duress or fraud.

Part payment of a debt
The rule in Pinnel's Case (1602) and Foakes v Beer (1884) 9 App Cas 605 is that paying less than the debt does not discharge the balance unless something new is given (earlier payment at the creditor's request, a different thing, a different place). Re Selectmove Ltd [1995] 1 WLR 474 refused to extend Roffey to part payment, because that would leave Foakes without effect. In MWB Business Exchange Centres Ltd v Rock Advertising Ltd [2018] UKSC 24 the Supreme Court decided the case on a no-oral-modification clause and left the Roffey and Foakes question open.

Promissory estoppel
- Origin: Hughes v Metropolitan Railway (1877) 2 App Cas 439; revived in Central London Property Trust v High Trees House Ltd [1947] KB 130.
- Requirements: a clear and unequivocal promise not to enforce strict rights; reliance by the promisee; and it must be inequitable for the promisor to go back. Where the promise was extracted by pressure, it is not inequitable to go back (D & C Builders v Rees [1966] 2 QB 617).
- It is a shield, not a sword: it cannot create a new cause of action (Combe v Combe [1951] 2 KB 215).
- Usually suspensory for ongoing payments, which can be revived on reasonable notice (Tool Metal Manufacturing Co v Tungsten Electric Co [1955] 1 WLR 761).

Intention to create legal relations
- Domestic and social agreements are presumed not to be intended as binding (Balfour v Balfour [1919] 2 KB 571), but the presumption can be rebutted, e.g. by separated spouses (Merritt v Merritt [1970] 1 WLR 1211).
- Commercial agreements are presumed binding; rebutting this is a heavy burden (Edwards v Skyways [1964] 1 WLR 349). An express "honour clause" can do it (Rose and Frank Co v JR Crompton & Bros [1925] AC 445).

Exam tips: in variation problems, work through Stilk, Roffey (practical benefit, no duress), then Foakes and promissory estoppel for debts. Duress links this topic to the duress topic.

notes.h: Interpretation, implied terms and statutory control
notes.body:
Once a contract exists, disputes are mostly about what it means. The Consumer Rights Act 2015 is on the LL142 indicative reading for 2026/27, alongside the judge-made rules of interpretation.

The modern approach to interpretation
- The court asks what a reasonable person, with all the background knowledge reasonably available to the parties when they contracted, would understand the words to mean (Investors Compensation Scheme Ltd v West Bromwich Building Society [1998] 1 WLR 896, Lord Hoffmann).
- Evidence of prior negotiations and of what a party subjectively intended is excluded (Chartbrook Ltd v Persimmon Homes Ltd [2009] UKHL 38, which also allowed obvious drafting mistakes to be corrected by construction where it is clear what the parties meant).
- Where there are two possible meanings, the court prefers the one more consistent with business common sense (Rainy Sky SA v Kookmin Bank [2011] UKSC 50).
- But commercial common sense must not be used to rewrite clear words because a bargain turned out badly (Arnold v Britton [2015] UKSC 36, where a service charge escalating at 10% a year was enforced as written).
- Textual and contextual analysis are tools, not rival theories; the weight given to each depends on the contract (Wood v Capita Insurance Services Ltd [2017] UKSC 24).

Implied terms
- In fact: a term is implied only if necessary for business efficacy or so obvious it goes without saying (The Moorcock (1889) 14 PD 64; the "officious bystander" of Shirlaw v Southern Foundries [1939] 2 KB 206). Marks and Spencer plc v BNP Paribas [2015] UKSC 72 confirmed that the test is necessity, not reasonableness, and that implied terms cannot contradict express terms.
- In law: terms implied into every contract of a defined type, e.g. landlord's duty to take reasonable care of common parts of a tower block (Liverpool City Council v Irwin [1977] AC 239).
- By statute: in consumer contracts the Consumer Rights Act 2015 treats goods as required to be of satisfactory quality (s 9), fit for a particular purpose made known (s 10) and as described (s 11), and services as performed with reasonable care and skill (s 49). Between businesses, the Sale of Goods Act 1979 ss 13 to 15 apply.

Incorporation and exemption clauses
- A signed document binds the signer whether read or not (L'Estrange v F Graucob Ltd [1934] 2 KB 394).
- Unsigned terms need reasonable notice before or at the time of contracting (Olley v Marlborough Court Ltd [1949] 1 KB 532); particularly onerous or unusual terms need especially clear notice (Interfoto Picture Library v Stiletto Visual Programmes [1989] QB 433; Thornton v Shoe Lane Parking [1971] 2 QB 163).

Statutory control
- Unfair Contract Terms Act 1977 (business contracts): liability for death or personal injury caused by negligence cannot be excluded (s 2(1)); other negligence liability can be excluded only if reasonable (s 2(2), with the test in s 11).
- Consumer Rights Act 2015, Part 2: an unfair term is not binding on the consumer (s 62(1)). A term is unfair if, contrary to good faith, it causes a significant imbalance in the parties' rights and obligations to the consumer's detriment (s 62(4)). The main subject matter and price cannot be assessed for fairness if the term is transparent and prominent (s 64). A trader cannot exclude liability for death or personal injury caused by negligence (s 65), or the statutory rights in ss 9 to 11 (s 31).

Policy questions
Is a contextual approach fairer, or does it make outcomes less predictable and litigation dearer? Should consumers and businesses be treated so differently?

Exam tips: for interpretation essays, set the ICS-Rainy Sky line against Arnold and Wood; for problem questions, check incorporation first, then construction, then UCTA or the CRA.

Misrepresentation is one of the two defences named in the LL142 course guide for 2026/27. It makes a contract voidable and may also give a right to damages.

Definition
An actionable misrepresentation is an unambiguous false statement of existing fact or law, made by one party to the other, which induces the other to enter the contract.

Statement of fact, not opinion or future intention
- A genuine opinion by someone with no special knowledge is not a statement of fact (Bisset v Wilkinson [1927] AC 177, PC: estimate of how many sheep untested land could carry).
- An opinion from someone who knows the facts can imply that there are facts justifying it (Smith v Land and House Property Corp (1884) 28 Ch D 7: a tenant described as "most desirable" who was behind with rent).
- A statement of present intention is a statement of fact about the speaker's state of mind, so a false one is actionable (Edgington v Fitzmaurice (1885) 29 Ch D 459).

Silence and conduct
- There is generally no duty to disclose (Keates v Cadogan (1851)).
- But a half-truth can be a misrepresentation (Dimmock v Hallett (1866) LR 2 Ch App 21), and so can failing to correct a statement that becomes untrue before the contract is made (With v O'Flanagan [1936] Ch 575).
- Conduct can amount to a representation (Spice Girls Ltd v Aprilia World Service BV [2002] EWCA Civ 15).

Inducement
- The statement must have induced the contract, though it need not be the only cause (Edgington).
- A claimant who relied on their own checks rather than the statement cannot claim (Attwood v Small (1838)).
- It is no defence that the claimant could have discovered the truth (Redgrave v Hurd (1881) 20 Ch D 1).
- A representee need not believe the statement is true; suspecting it might be false does not bar a claim if they were in fact induced (Hayward v Zurich Insurance Co plc [2016] UKSC 48, a case of fraudulent misrepresentation).

Types and damages
- Fraudulent: made knowingly, without belief in its truth, or recklessly, careless whether it is true or false (Derry v Peek (1889) 14 App Cas 337). Damages in the tort of deceit cover all losses flowing directly from the fraud, foreseeable or not (Smith New Court Securities v Scrimgeour Vickers [1997] AC 254).
- Negligent at common law: under Hedley Byrne v Heller [1964] AC 465 where there is a special relationship (applied to pre-contract statements in Esso Petroleum v Mardon [1976] QB 801).
- Under the Misrepresentation Act 1967, s 2(1): the representor is liable unless they prove they had reasonable grounds to believe, and did believe, the statement was true up to the time of the contract. Damages are assessed as if the representation were fraudulent (Royscot Trust Ltd v Rogerson [1991] 2 QB 297), which is much criticised.
- Innocent: rescission, with the court able to award damages instead of rescission under s 2(2).

Rescission and its bars
Rescission sets the contract aside and restores both parties to their former positions. It can be done by notifying the other party; where a fraudster disappears, telling the police can be enough (Car and Universal Finance Co v Caldwell [1965] 1 QB 525). It is barred by:
- affirmation after learning the truth;
- lapse of time (Leaf v International Galleries [1950] 2 KB 86: five years for a painting);
- intervening third-party rights acquired in good faith for value;
- impossibility of restoring the parties to their original positions (though courts allow substantial rather than precise restoration).

Excluding liability
A term excluding liability for misrepresentation in a business contract must satisfy the reasonableness test (Misrepresentation Act 1967, s 3, applying UCTA s 11). In consumer contracts, the Consumer Rights Act 2015 fairness rules apply instead.

Exam tips: work through statement, fact, inducement, type, then remedy; always consider s 2(1) because the reversed burden makes it the claimant's best route.

Duress is the second named defence in the LL142 course guide for 2026/27, which lists Stephen A Smith, "Contracting Under Pressure: A Theory of Duress" [1997] CLJ 343 as reading. Contracts made under duress are voidable.

Forms of duress
- Duress to the person: threats of violence. In Barton v Armstrong [1976] AC 104 (PC) the threat needed only to be one reason for entering the contract.
- Duress of goods: threats to seize, damage or withhold property; accepted (obiter) as capable of making a contract voidable in The Siboen and the Sibotre.
- Economic duress: illegitimate commercial pressure. The modern doctrine grew from cases including The Siboen and the Sibotre [1976] 1 Lloyd's Rep 293, North Ocean Shipping v Hyundai (The Atlantic Baron) [1979] QB 705 and Pao On v Lau Yiu Long [1980] AC 614.

The elements
In Pakistan International Airline Corp v Times Travel (UK) Ltd [2021] UKSC 40 Lord Burrows set out three elements:
- an illegitimate threat or pressure (Dimskal Shipping Co v ITWF (The Evia Luck) [1992] 2 AC 152);
- which caused the claimant to enter the contract (The Evia Luck speaks of a "significant cause"; for economic duress this means a "but for" cause: Huyton SA v Peter Cremer GmbH [1999] 1 Lloyd's Rep 620);
- the claimant had no reasonable alternative but to give in (Lord Burrows relied on DSND Subsea, below, for this element).

Threatened breach of contract
Threatening to break a contract is often illegitimate. In Atlas Express v Kafco [1989] QB 833 a carrier refused to carry goods unless the customer agreed a higher price; the customer, which could not find another carrier in time and depended on a major retail contract, was not bound. In DSND Subsea Ltd v Petroleum Geo-Services ASA [2000] BLR 530 Dyson J listed factors: whether there was an actual or threatened breach, whether the party acted in good or bad faith, whether there was a realistic alternative, whether the victim protested, and whether the victim later affirmed.

Lawful act duress
A threat to do something lawful (such as refusing to deal) is rarely illegitimate. CTN Cash and Carry v Gallaher [1994] 4 All ER 714 held there was no duress where a supplier threatened to withdraw credit to obtain payment it honestly believed was owed. In Times Travel the airline, the only operator of direct flights to Pakistan, gave a small Birmingham travel agent notice ending their arrangement and cut its fortnightly ticket allocation from 300 to 60; the agent then signed a new agreement waiving its claims to unpaid commission. The majority (Lord Hodge, with whom Lord Reed, Lord Lloyd-Jones and Lord Kitchin agreed) held that lawful act duress exists but is confined to conduct that equity has recognised as reprehensible, in two main situations: using knowledge of the claimant's (or a close relative's) criminal conduct to extract a benefit; and, where the defendant faces a civil claim, using reprehensible means to put the claimant in a vulnerable position so that it gives up the claim. The airline's conduct was hard bargaining, not duress. Lord Burrows agreed with the result but would have asked whether the threatening party deliberately created or increased the claimant's vulnerability and made its demand in bad faith.

Affirmation
A victim who does not protest and goes on with the contract once the pressure ends may be taken to have affirmed it (The Atlantic Baron: eight months' delay).

Theories of duress
Early cases spoke of the victim's will being "overborne"; later cases, such as The Universe Sentinel [1983] 1 AC 366, focus on whether the pressure was illegitimate, because a victim usually chooses deliberately. Smith's 1997 article examines how a theory should account for wrongful pressure and the victim's choice.

Related doctrines
- Undue influence: an abuse of a relationship of influence or of actual pressure. In Royal Bank of Scotland v Etridge (No 2) [2001] UKHL 44 the House of Lords explained how influence can be proved and what banks must do when a wife guarantees her husband's debts.
- Duress also links with consideration: Williams v Roffey upheld the extra promise partly because it was not obtained by duress.

Exam tips: for a renegotiation problem, analyse both consideration (Roffey) and duress; apply the Times Travel elements in order, and finish with affirmation.

Breach is a failure, without lawful excuse, to perform a contractual obligation when due. Liability is usually strict: it does not matter that the party tried hard, unless the term only requires reasonable care (as in most service contracts).

Which breaches allow termination?
Every breach gives a right to damages. Only a repudiatory breach also allows the innocent party to terminate. Whether a breach is repudiatory depends on the kind of term broken.
- Conditions: important terms whose breach allows termination, however small the consequences. Poussard v Spiers (1876) 1 QBD 410 (singer missing the opening nights: condition) contrasts with Bettini v Gye (1876) 1 QBD 183 (singer missing rehearsals: warranty). Under the Sale of Goods Act 1979, ss 13 to 15 are conditions, and strict compliance with description is required (Arcos Ltd v EA Ronaasen & Son [1933] AC 470), though for business buyers s 15A stops rejection for a slight breach.
- Warranties: less important terms; breach gives damages only.
- Innominate terms: whether termination is allowed depends on whether the breach deprives the innocent party of substantially the whole benefit of the contract (Hongkong Fir Shipping Co v Kawasaki Kisen Kaisha [1962] 2 QB 26, unseaworthy ship; Cehave v Bremer (The Hansa Nord) [1976] QB 44).
- Calling a term a "condition" does not settle the matter if the parties cannot sensibly have meant it (Schuler AG v Wickman Machine Tool Sales [1974] AC 235). In commercial contracts, time clauses are often conditions for certainty (Bunge Corp v Tradax Export SA [1981] 1 WLR 711).

Anticipatory breach
If a party, before performance is due, clearly shows it will not perform, the innocent party may terminate and sue at once (Hochster v De la Tour (1853) 2 E & B 678) or affirm and wait. Affirming is risky: if a frustrating event then occurs, the right to sue may be lost (Avery v Bowden (1855)). After affirming, a party cannot later rely on the earlier repudiation alone (Fercometal SARL v Mediterranean Shipping Co [1989] AC 788).

Electing to terminate or affirm
- Termination must be clearly communicated, though in some cases conduct such as not performing can be enough (Vitol SA v Norelf Ltd (The Santa Clara) [1996] AC 800).
- Termination operates for the future only: accrued rights survive, and so do clauses meant to govern the consequences of breach, such as exclusion clauses (Photo Production Ltd v Securicor Transport Ltd [1980] AC 827).
- An innocent party who can perform without the other's cooperation may affirm, perform and claim the price (White and Carter (Councils) Ltd v McGregor [1962] AC 413), unless it has no legitimate interest in doing so.

Entire obligations
Where payment depends on complete performance, partial performance earns nothing (Cutter v Powell (1795); Sumpter v Hedges [1898] 1 QB 673), but substantial performance of a lump-sum contract allows recovery less the cost of putting defects right (Hoenig v Isaacs [1952] 2 All ER 176).

Consumer contracts
Under the Consumer Rights Act 2015 a consumer whose goods do not conform has a short-term right to reject, normally within 30 days (ss 20 and 22), then a right to repair or replacement (s 23), then a price reduction or final right to reject (s 24).

Exam tips: classify the term (condition, warranty or innominate), decide whether the breach is repudiatory, then advise on the election and its risks.

Damages are the normal remedy for breach and are available as of right. The basic aim is to put the claimant, so far as money can, in the position they would have been in if the contract had been performed (Robinson v Harman (1848) 1 Exch 850).

Measures of loss
- Expectation: the value of performance, e.g. lost profit or the difference between contract and market price.
- Reliance: wasted expenditure, including expenditure before the contract if it was in the parties' contemplation (Anglia Television Ltd v Reed [1972] 1 QB 60). A claimant cannot use reliance damages to escape a bad bargain (C & P Haulage v Middleton [1983] 1 WLR 1461).
- Cost of cure or difference in value? In Ruxley Electronics and Construction Ltd v Forsyth [1996] AC 344 a pool was built shallower than agreed but was still safe and its value was unchanged. Rebuilding (costing more than £21,000) was out of all proportion to the benefit, so the House of Lords restored the trial judge's award of £2,500 for loss of amenity, reversing the Court of Appeal's award of the cost of rebuilding.

Remoteness
- Hadley v Baxendale (1854) 9 Exch 341: recoverable losses are those arising naturally from the breach (limb one) or those that both parties may reasonably be supposed to have contemplated, when they contracted, as a probable result of breach (limb two, usually based on special knowledge communicated to the defendant).
- Victoria Laundry (Windsor) Ltd v Newman Industries Ltd [1949] 2 KB 528: ordinary lost profits from a late boiler were recoverable, but especially lucrative dyeing contracts unknown to the defendant were not.
- The Heron II (Koufos v C Czarnikow Ltd) [1969] 1 AC 350: contract requires a higher degree of likelihood ("not unlikely") than tort's reasonable foreseeability.
- If the type of loss was within contemplation, its extent need not have been (Parsons (Livestock) Ltd v Uttley Ingham & Co [1978] QB 791).
- Transfield Shipping Inc v Mercator Shipping Inc (The Achilleas) [2008] UKHL 48: some judges asked whether the defendant should be taken to have assumed responsibility for the type of loss in question, given the market understanding. Later cases treat this as relevant mainly in unusual cases.

Mitigation
The claimant cannot recover loss that could have been avoided by reasonable steps (British Westinghouse Electric v Underground Electric Railways [1912] AC 673). In Payzu Ltd v Saunders [1919] 2 KB 581 a buyer should have accepted the seller's offer to keep supplying for cash. Reasonable costs of mitigating are recoverable.

Non-pecuniary loss
Generally not recoverable for disappointment or distress (Addis v Gramophone Co [1909] AC 488), except where a major or important object of the contract was to give pleasure, relaxation or peace of mind (Jarvis v Swans Tours [1973] QB 233, holidays; Farley v Skinner [2001] UKHL 49, a surveyor asked to check aircraft noise).

Gain-based awards
- An account of profits is exceptional and only where ordinary remedies are inadequate and the claimant has a legitimate interest in preventing profit-making (Attorney General v Blake [2001] 1 AC 268, a former spy's memoirs).
- Negotiating damages (sometimes called Wrotham Park damages, after Wrotham Park Estate Co v Parkside Homes [1974] 1 WLR 798) value what a reasonable release of the right would have cost. Morris-Garner v One Step (Support) Ltd [2018] UKSC 20 held that they are available only where the breach has caused the loss of a valuable asset created or protected by the right, such as a restrictive covenant over land or intellectual property, not where ordinary financial loss can be proved.

Policy debate
The course asks whether contract law should focus so strongly on the expectation interest. Ruxley's consumer surplus and Blake's account of profits both test the line between compensation and protecting performance.

Exam tips: identify the interest claimed, then work through remoteness, mitigation and any non-pecuniary heads; quote Robinson v Harman as your starting point.

notes.h: Specific performance, injunctions, agreed sums and penalties
notes.body:
Co-operative Insurance Society Ltd v Argyll Stores (Holdings) Ltd [1998] AC 1 (HL) is on the LL142 indicative reading for 2026/27. It is the leading modern case on when equity will order a party to perform.

Specific performance
Specific performance is an equitable remedy, so it is discretionary. It is ordered mainly where damages are inadequate.
- Land is treated as unique, so contracts to sell land are routinely specifically enforced.
- Goods: only if specific or ascertained and effectively unique (court's power in the Sale of Goods Act 1979, s 52; Falcke v Gray (1859), rare china jars).
- Inadequacy can come from the remedy's structure: in Beswick v Beswick [1968] AC 58 the widow, as administratrix, obtained specific performance of the promise to pay her an annuity because the estate's damages would have been nominal.

Bars and discretionary factors
- Co-op v Argyll: the House of Lords refused to order a supermarket anchor tenant to keep trading under a keep-open covenant. Reasons: it would require the court's continued supervision of carrying on a business; enforcement would be by contempt, a blunt weapon; it could cause the defendant losses far greater than the claimant's; and settled practice was against it.
- Contracts for personal services are not specifically enforced (and no court may compel an employee to work: Trade Union and Labour Relations (Consolidation) Act 1992, s 236).
- Other factors: hardship, the claimant's own conduct ("clean hands"), delay, lack of mutuality.
- The court may award damages in addition to or in substitution for specific performance (Senior Courts Act 1981, s 50, originally Lord Cairns' Act 1858).
- Consumers: the court may order specific performance of the trader's repair or replacement duties (Consumer Rights Act 2015, s 58).

Injunctions
A prohibitory injunction can enforce a negative promise. In Lumley v Wagner (1852) a singer was restrained from singing elsewhere. Warner Bros Pictures v Nelson [1937] 1 KB 209 enforced an actress's promise not to act for others, because she could earn a living in other work. But no injunction will be granted if it would in practice force the defendant to perform personal services (Page One Records v Britton [1968] 1 WLR 157, a band's manager).

Action for an agreed sum
A claim for the price or another sum due is a debt claim, not damages, so remoteness and mitigation do not apply. White and Carter v McGregor [1962] AC 413 allowed an advertiser to perform and claim the full price after the customer repudiated, subject to the "legitimate interest" limit.

Agreed damages and penalties
Parties often fix the sum payable on breach. The penalty rule strikes down clauses that go too far.
- Old test: was the sum a genuine pre-estimate of loss, or a deterrent (Dunlop Pneumatic Tyre Co v New Garage [1915] AC 79)?
- New test: Cavendish Square Holding BV v Makdessi; ParkingEye Ltd v Beavis [2015] UKSC 67. A clause is penal if it is a secondary obligation that imposes a detriment on the contract-breaker out of all proportion to any legitimate interest of the innocent party in the enforcement of the primary obligation.
- In ParkingEye an £85 overstay charge was upheld: the operator and landowner had a legitimate interest in managing parking that went beyond compensation.
- The rule applies only to obligations triggered by breach, not to primary obligations such as a price.

Policy question
Should specific performance be the primary remedy, as in many civil law systems, so that promisees get what they bargained for? Supporters of Co-op v Argyll point to cost and practicality; critics say it lets a defendant buy its way out of a promise.

Exam tips: in any remedies problem, check whether damages are adequate before discussing specific performance, then apply the discretionary bars; for agreed sums, apply Makdessi's legitimate-interest test.

A properly posted acceptance is effective on posting (Adams v Lindsell, 1818), unless the offeror excludes it, e.g. by requiring actual notice (Holwell Securities v Hughes, 1974).
Effective only when communicated to the offeree (Byrne v Van Tienhoven, 1880); can be communicated by a reliable third party (Dickinson v Dodds, 1876).
Battle of the forms: applying offer, counter-offer and acceptance, the last set of terms sent before acceptance or performance usually wins.
A contract can be formed by conduct even where the parties' documents said 'subject to contract', if the parties are found to have waived that condition.
Some right, interest, profit or benefit to one party, or some forbearance, detriment, loss or responsibility given, suffered or undertaken by the other.
Consideration need not be adequate: chocolate wrappers, even if thrown away, formed part of the consideration.
CA: a promise to pay extra for existing contractual work can be binding if the promisor gets a practical benefit and there is no economic duress or fraud.
HL: part payment of a debt does not discharge the balance; the creditor can still claim the rest (following Pinnel's Case).
CA refused to apply Roffey's practical benefit to promises to accept part payment of a debt, as Foakes v Beer binds.
Clear and unequivocal promise not to enforce strict rights, reliance by the promisee, and inequitable for the promisor to go back (High Trees; D & C Builders v Rees).
Promissory estoppel is a shield, not a sword: it cannot create a new cause of action where there is no consideration.
Agreements between spouses living together are presumed not intended to be legally binding; rebuttable (Merritt v Merritt, separated spouses).
HL: contracts mean what a reasonable person with the parties' background knowledge would understand; prior negotiations and subjective intent excluded.
Natural meaning of clear words prevails; commercial common sense cannot be used to rescue a party from a bargain that turned out badly.
UKSC: where words have more than one possible meaning, prefer the one most consistent with business common sense.
Textualism and contextualism are complementary tools, not conflicting doctrines; their weight depends on the contract.
A term is implied in fact only if necessary for business efficacy or so obvious it goes without saying; reasonableness is not enough.
Term implied in law into tenancies of a tower block: landlord to take reasonable care to maintain common parts.
An unfair term is not binding on the consumer. Unfair = contrary to good faith, causes significant imbalance in rights and obligations to the consumer's detriment.
s 2(1): cannot exclude liability for death or personal injury from negligence. s 2(2): other negligence liability excludable only if reasonable (s 11).
An unambiguous false statement of existing fact or law, made by one party to the other, that induces the other to enter the contract.
PC: an honest opinion about sheep capacity of untested land, given by someone with no special knowledge, was not a statement of fact.
A false statement of present intention is a misstatement of fact; the misrepresentation need not be the sole inducement.
A statement true when made but which becomes false before the contract must be corrected; failure to do so is misrepresentation.
Fraud = statement made knowingly, without belief in its truth, or recklessly careless whether it is true or false.
Liability for non-fraudulent misrepresentation unless the representor proves reasonable grounds to believe and actual belief up to the contract. Damages as for fraud (Royscot).
Rescission for innocent misrepresentation barred by lapse of time: buyer of a painting claimed five years later.
A representee need not believe the representation is true to be induced by it; suspicion of falsity does not bar a claim (a fraud case).
As set out by Lord Burrows: an illegitimate threat or pressure; causation; and the claimant had no reasonable alternative but to submit (DSND Subsea).
PC: duress to the person; threat of death need only be one reason for entering the contract.
Carrier's threat to stop deliveries unless paid more amounted to economic duress; customer had no practical alternative, so renegotiated price unenforceable.
Threat must be a 'but for' cause of entering the contract (Huyton v Peter Cremer, 1999), stricter than for duress to the person.
Rare. Times Travel [2021] UKSC 40: confined to recognised categories of reprehensible conduct; hard bargaining with lawful threats is not enough.
Economic duress found, but the buyer affirmed: it made later payments and took delivery without further protest, then waited about eight months before claiming.

cards.f: CTN Cash and Carry v Gallaher [1994]
cards.b: No duress where a supplier lawfully threatened to withdraw credit to get payment it honestly believed was due.
A term whose breach entitles the innocent party to terminate as well as claim damages, whatever the consequences (e.g. Poussard v Spiers).
A minor term whose breach gives only damages, not a right to terminate (e.g. Bettini v Gye).
Innominate terms: termination allowed only if the breach deprives the innocent party of substantially the whole benefit of the contract.
Anticipatory breach: the innocent party can terminate and sue at once, without waiting for the date for performance.
Termination for breach operates prospectively; exclusion clauses still apply. No rule of law that 'fundamental breach' destroys an exclusion clause.
Innocent party may affirm, perform and claim the price if it needs no cooperation, unless it has no legitimate interest in doing so.
Calling a term a 'condition' is not conclusive; a court may decide the parties did not intend any breach to allow termination.
Consumer may reject non-conforming goods, normally within 30 days (ss 20, 22); then repair/replacement (s 23); then price reduction or final rejection (s 24).
Contract damages aim to put the claimant, so far as money can, in the position as if the contract had been performed (expectation).
Cost of cure refused where out of all proportion to the benefit (pool slightly too shallow); HL restored the trial judge's £2,500 for loss of amenity.
Remoteness: losses arising naturally from the breach, or within both parties' reasonable contemplation when contracting as probable results.
Ordinary lost profits recoverable; exceptionally lucrative dyeing contracts unknown to the defendant were too remote.
Contract remoteness requires loss to be 'not unlikely' (a serious possibility), a stricter test than tort's reasonable foreseeability.
Claimant cannot recover loss reasonable steps would have avoided (British Westinghouse, 1912; Payzu v Saunders, 1919).
Non-pecuniary damages recoverable where an important object of the contract was pleasure or peace of mind (surveyor asked about aircraft noise).
HL: account of profits for breach of contract available exceptionally, when other remedies are inadequate and claimant has a legitimate interest.
HL refused specific performance of a keep-open covenant: constant supervision, contempt as blunt weapon, disproportionate loss to defendant, settled practice.
Discretionary; mainly where damages are inadequate, e.g. land or unique goods; refused for personal services or where supervision or hardship problems arise.
Specific performance ordered in favour of a widow as administratrix because damages to the estate would have been nominal and inadequate.
Injunction enforced an actress's negative covenant not to work for rival studios, as she could still earn a living in other ways.
Is the secondary obligation out of all proportion to the innocent party's legitimate interest in enforcing the primary obligation? If so, unenforceable.
£85 overstay charge not a penalty: legitimate interest in managing car park went beyond compensating for loss.
Court may award damages in addition to, or in substitution for, an injunction or specific performance (Lord Cairns' Act jurisdiction).

questions.q: Lara puts a jar of honey labelled £6 in her basket in a self-service shop. At the till the assistant says the label is wrong and the price is £9. On the classic analysis, which statement is right?
options: The shop made an offer at £6, which Lara accepts at the till, so the shop must sell at £6
There can be no contract until Lara has paid and left the shop
The shop made an offer by labelling the honey, which Lara accepted by putting it in her basket
Lara makes an offer at the till, which the shop is free to refuse
questions.why: Boots treats goods on shelves as an invitation to treat, so the customer makes the offer at the till and the shop may reject it. Treating the label as an offer accepted when goods go into the basket is the position Boots rejected (it would stop customers changing their minds). Saying the offer is accepted at the till makes the same mistake about who offers. Saying there is no contract until she leaves confuses formation with payment: the contract is made when the cashier accepts her offer.

questions.q: On Monday V emails an offer to sell a painting for £2,000. On Tuesday P replies 'I'll pay £1,800'. V refuses. On Wednesday P writes 'Fine, I accept £2,000'. Is there a contract?
options: No, because P's Tuesday reply was a counter-offer that destroyed the original offer, so Wednesday's message is only a fresh offer
Yes, because P accepted the original offer before V withdrew it
No, because emailed acceptances only take effect when read
Yes, because a request to vary the price is only a request for information
questions.why: Under Hyde v Wrench a counter-offer rejects the original offer; P's Wednesday letter is a new offer that V may accept or reject. Saying P accepted before withdrawal ignores that the offer had already been destroyed. A proposal of a lower price is a counter-offer, not a request for information as in Stevenson v McLean, where the offeree only asked whether delivery terms could be varied. Timing of emails is irrelevant because there was no live offer to accept.

questions.q: Explain, with authority, when an acceptance sent by post takes effect, and two situations in which the postal rule does not apply. (5 marks)
markScheme: Postal acceptance takes effect on posting: Adams v Lindsell (1818)
Rule applies only where use of post is reasonable/contemplated and the letter is properly posted
Offeror can exclude it, e.g. requiring 'notice in writing' (Holwell Securities v Hughes, 1974)
Does not apply to instantaneous communications, which take effect on receipt (Entores; Brinkibon)
Does not apply to revocation, which must be received (Byrne v Van Tienhoven)
questions.modelAnswer: Under the postal rule, an acceptance sent by post takes effect when it is properly posted, not when it arrives (Adams v Lindsell (1818)). This applies only where it was reasonable to accept by post and the letter was correctly addressed and stamped. The rule gives way to the offeror's terms: in Holwell Securities v Hughes (1974) an option to be exercised 'by notice in writing' required actual receipt, so a lost letter was not an acceptance. It also does not apply to instantaneous methods such as telex, where acceptance takes effect when and where it is received (Entores (1955); Brinkibon (1983)). Finally, it never applies to revocation of an offer, which must actually be communicated (Byrne v Van Tienhoven (1880)).

questions.q: B is building flats for D for a fixed price. B is in financial difficulty. D, worried about a late-completion penalty in its own contract with the owner, promises B an extra £10,000 to finish on time. B finishes. D refuses to pay the extra. Applying Williams v Roffey, which is the best answer?
options: D need not pay, because past consideration is no consideration
D must pay, because promissory estoppel can found a claim for the extra money
D must pay, because D obtained a practical benefit and there is no suggestion B extracted the promise by duress
D need not pay, because B only did what B was already contractually bound to do, as in Stilk v Myrick
questions.why: These are close to the Roffey facts: the promise was volunteered by D, who avoided a penalty and the cost of finding a new builder, so practical benefit is consideration. Relying on Stilk v Myrick alone ignores how Roffey limited it. The past-consideration rule is irrelevant: B's completion came after, and in return for, D's promise. Promissory estoppel cannot be used as a cause of action (Combe v Combe), so it cannot be the basis of B's claim.

questions.q: C owes £10,000, due today. The creditor agrees to accept £8,000 today in full settlement. Later the creditor sues for £2,000. Which is the most accurate statement of the common law position?
options: The creditor can recover, because part payment of a debt on the due date is not consideration for releasing the balance (Foakes v Beer)
The creditor can recover only if the agreement was made in writing
The creditor cannot recover, because the creditor obtained a practical benefit, as in Williams v Roffey
The creditor cannot recover, because any agreement to vary a contract is binding without consideration
questions.why: Foakes v Beer (applying Pinnel's Case) holds that paying less on the due date gives no consideration for the release. Re Selectmove refused to apply Roffey's practical-benefit idea to part payment of debts, so the Roffey answer is wrong. Variations generally need consideration (or a deed), so saying any variation is binding is wrong. Writing is not what matters; consideration is. Promissory estoppel might help C in equity, but that is a different question from the common law position asked about.

questions.q: Explain the requirements of promissory estoppel and two limits on it. (5 marks)
markScheme: Clear and unequivocal promise/representation not to enforce strict legal rights (Hughes v Metropolitan Railway; High Trees)
Reliance by the promisee (detriment not strictly required)
Inequitable for promisor to go back; not where promise obtained by pressure (D & C Builders v Rees)
Shield not sword: cannot found a cause of action (Combe v Combe)
Usually suspensory; rights can be revived on reasonable notice (Tool Metal Manufacturing v Tungsten Electric)
questions.modelAnswer: Promissory estoppel, from Hughes v Metropolitan Railway (1877) and High Trees (1947), stops a promisor going back on a clear and unequivocal promise not to enforce strict legal rights where the promisee has relied on it and it would be inequitable to allow the promisor to go back. In D & C Builders v Rees (1966) it did not help a debtor who had pressured the creditor into accepting less, because the debtor had not acted equitably. Two limits: first, it is a shield not a sword, so it cannot create a cause of action where there is no consideration (Combe v Combe (1951)). Second, its effect is usually suspensory for continuing obligations: the promisor can restore strict rights for the future by giving reasonable notice (Tool Metal Manufacturing v Tungsten Electric (1955)).

questions.q: Which statement best reflects Arnold v Britton [2015] UKSC 36?
options: Where a result seems commercially unwise, the court should prefer a meaning that avoids it even if the words are clear
Evidence of pre-contract negotiations is admissible to show what the parties meant
Implied terms can override express terms if that produces a fairer result
Where words are clear, the court will not depart from their natural meaning just because the result is commercially unwise for one party
questions.why: In Arnold the Supreme Court enforced a service charge clause that escalated at 10% a year because the words were clear. Using commercial sense to override clear words reads Rainy Sky too broadly; Rainy Sky only helps choose between possible meanings. Prior negotiations are excluded (Chartbrook). Implied terms cannot contradict express ones (M&S v BNP Paribas).

questions.q: A hotel guest signs the register at reception. On entering her room she sees a notice excluding the hotel's liability for stolen goods. Her furs are stolen through the hotel's negligence. Is the exclusion incorporated?
options: No, because the notice was seen only after the contract had been made at reception
Yes, because she signed the register
No, because exclusion clauses are never valid against negligence
Yes, because notices in rooms are always incorporated by a course of dealing
questions.why: These are the facts of Olley v Marlborough Court: the contract was made at reception, so a later notice could not be part of it. Signing the register does not help the hotel, because the register did not contain the term (L'Estrange applies only to signed contractual documents). There was no consistent course of dealing on these facts. Exclusion of negligence liability is possible if clearly worded and incorporated (subject to UCTA or the CRA), so saying it is never valid overstates the law.

questions.q: Explain when a court will imply a term in fact, with reference to Marks and Spencer plc v BNP Paribas [2015] UKSC 72. (5 marks)
markScheme: Implication in fact is about the presumed intention of these parties
Test: necessary for business efficacy (The Moorcock) or so obvious it goes without saying (Shirlaw officious bystander)
M&S v BNP: necessity, not reasonableness or fairness; either limb can suffice
Term must be capable of clear expression and cannot contradict express terms
Applied: no implied term to refund rent paid in advance for the period after a break date
questions.modelAnswer: Terms are implied in fact to give effect to what these particular parties must have intended. The term must be necessary to give the contract business efficacy (The Moorcock (1889)) or so obvious that it goes without saying (the officious bystander test in Shirlaw v Southern Foundries (1939)). In Marks and Spencer v BNP Paribas (2015), the Supreme Court stressed that the test is necessity, not reasonableness: a court will not imply a term just because it would be fair or the parties would have agreed to it if asked. The term must be capable of clear expression and must not contradict any express term. Applying this, the court refused to imply a term requiring the landlord to refund rent paid in advance for the period after the tenant exercised a break clause.

questions.q: During negotiations to sell a medical practice, S truthfully says it earns £2,000 a year. Months later, but before the contract is signed, the income drops sharply because S is ill. S says nothing. The buyer completes. What is the best analysis?
options: No misrepresentation, because the statement was true when made
No misrepresentation, because silence can never be a misrepresentation
Misrepresentation, because S had to correct the statement once it became untrue before the contract
Misrepresentation only if S was fraudulent
questions.why: These are the facts of With v O'Flanagan: a representation continues until the contract, so S had to correct it. Testing truth only at the moment the statement was made ignores that continuing duty. The general rule of no duty to disclose has exceptions, including this one and half-truths, so 'never' is wrong. Fraud is not needed: the misrepresentation exists whatever S's state of mind, which matters only for the type of damages.

questions.q: Which statement best describes damages under s 2(1) of the Misrepresentation Act 1967 as interpreted in Royscot Trust v Rogerson?
options: No damages are available; the only remedy is rescission
Damages are limited to foreseeable losses as in the tort of negligence
Damages are assessed on the tort of deceit measure, covering all direct losses even if unforeseeable
Damages are assessed as in contract, putting the claimant in the position as if the statement were true
questions.why: Royscot read the 'fiction of fraud' in s 2(1) literally: damages are as for deceit, covering all direct loss. The contract measure is wrong because misrepresentation damages are tortious, not about making the statement true. The negligence measure is what many critics think the law should be, but it is not what Royscot decided. The 'rescission only' answer describes innocent misrepresentation without the s 2(2) discretion, not s 2(1).

questions.q: Outline the bars to rescission for misrepresentation, with one authority for each. (5 marks)
markScheme: Affirmation with knowledge of the misrepresentation (e.g. Long v Lloyd)
Lapse of time, especially for innocent misrepresentation (Leaf v International Galleries)
Intervening third-party rights acquired in good faith for value before rescission (cf. Car and Universal Finance v Caldwell, where rescission came first)
Impossibility of restitutio in integrum, applied flexibly
Court's discretion to award damages in lieu under Misrepresentation Act 1967 s 2(2)
questions.modelAnswer: Rescission is lost in four main situations. First, affirmation: if the claimant, knowing of the misrepresentation, acts in a way that shows an intention to go on with the contract (as in Long v Lloyd (1958), where the buyer kept using a lorry after discovering defects). Second, lapse of time: in Leaf v International Galleries (1950) a buyer who discovered five years later that a painting was not a Constable could not rescind. Third, third-party rights: if an innocent third party buys the goods for value before the contract is rescinded, rescission is barred; in Car and Universal Finance v Caldwell (1965) the seller had already rescinded by telling the police, so a later buyer got no title. Fourth, if the parties cannot be substantially restored to their original positions. In addition, for non-fraudulent misrepresentation the court may refuse rescission and award damages instead under s 2(2) of the 1967 Act.

questions.q: Under Pakistan International Airline v Times Travel [2021] UKSC 40, which statement is correct about lawful act duress?
options: Any threat to do a lawful act is duress if the victim had no practical alternative
It does not exist in English law; only threats of unlawful acts can be duress
It applies whenever the stronger party has a monopoly position
It is confined to narrow categories of reprehensible conduct, and hard bargaining is not enough
questions.why: The Supreme Court accepted that lawful act duress exists but kept it narrow: an airline's lawful threat to stop dealing with an agent was not duress. Saying any lawful threat is enough if there is no alternative drops the illegitimacy requirement entirely. Saying it does not exist is wrong because the court recognised it, even though it did not apply. Monopoly power alone was the very feature of Times Travel's case that did not make the threat illegitimate.

questions.q: A shipbuilder threatens not to deliver a ship unless the buyer pays 10% more than agreed. The buyer pays under protest, takes delivery, and then says nothing for eight months before claiming the extra back. What is the most likely result?
options: The buyer cannot recover, because by its delay it affirmed the varied contract, even though there was duress
The buyer recovers only if the shipbuilder acted fraudulently
The buyer recovers, because the threat was economic duress
The buyer cannot recover, because the extra payment was supported by consideration
questions.why: This is The Atlantic Baron: duress was established, but the buyer's later delay without protest affirmed the contract. Saying the buyer recovers because there was duress stops before the affirmation step. In The Atlantic Baron the yard did give consideration (it increased its letter of credit), but that was not why the claim failed, and consideration does not cure duress. Fraud is not an element of duress.

questions.q: Explain the elements of economic duress, with authority. (5 marks)
markScheme: Pressure must be illegitimate (The Evia Luck); threatened breach of contract often is (Atlas Express v Kafco)
Causation: threat must be a 'but for' cause (Huyton v Peter Cremer)
No reasonable alternative (DSND Subsea; Lord Burrows in Times Travel)
Relevant factors: good/bad faith, protest, alternatives (DSND Subsea v PGS)
Remedy: contract voidable; bars include affirmation (The Atlantic Baron)
questions.modelAnswer: Economic duress makes a contract voidable where there was illegitimate pressure which caused the claimant to contract and left no reasonable alternative (the three elements set out by Lord Burrows in Times Travel (2021)). The pressure must be illegitimate (The Evia Luck (1992)), and a threatened breach of contract often is, as in Atlas Express v Kafco (1989), where a carrier threatened to stop deliveries unless paid more. Causation is stricter than for duress to the person: the threat must be a 'but for' cause (Huyton v Peter Cremer (1999)). The claimant must have had no reasonable alternative, such as suing or finding another supplier; in DSND Subsea v PGS (2000) Dyson J treated this as a factor alongside good or bad faith, protest and later affirmation. The remedy is rescission, which is lost by affirmation, as in The Atlantic Baron (1979).

questions.q: A two-year time charter contains an obligation to provide a 'seaworthy' ship. Because of old engines and an incompetent engine-room crew, the ship is out of service for about 20 weeks in the first months of the charter, but about 17 months of the charter remain once it is repaired. Can the charterer terminate?
options: No, because breach of an obligation of seaworthiness can only ever give damages
No, unless the delay deprived the charterer of substantially the whole benefit of the contract, which it did not
Yes, because seaworthiness is a condition and any breach allows termination
Yes, because any breach of contract allows termination if the innocent party gives notice
questions.why: Hongkong Fir held that the seaworthiness obligation is innominate, so termination depends on how serious the consequences are; losing about 20 weeks of a two-year charter, with most of the charter still to run, was not enough. Calling it a condition is the argument that failed in that case. Saying only damages are ever available ignores that a serious enough breach of an innominate term allows termination. Not every breach is repudiatory, so termination by notice for any breach is wrong.

questions.q: In January, X tells Y it will not perform a contract due in June. Y says it will keep the contract alive. In March, war makes performance illegal and frustrates the contract. What is Y's position?
options: Y can sue because frustration never affects anticipatory breach
Y can claim the full contract price under White and Carter v McGregor
Y can sue for damages for the January repudiation because the breach happened first
Y has lost the right to sue for the repudiation, because by affirming it kept the contract alive for both sides and the contract was then frustrated
questions.why: This follows Avery v Bowden: by affirming, Y kept the contract alive, so it was frustrated before any actual breach and X was discharged. Saying Y can sue because the repudiation came first forgets that Y did not accept it. Saying frustration never affects anticipatory breach is the same mistake stated as a rule. White and Carter lets an innocent party who can perform without cooperation earn the price, but here performance became illegal, so Y could not perform.

questions.q: Distinguish conditions, warranties and innominate terms, with one case for each. (5 marks)
markScheme: Condition: breach gives right to terminate and damages whatever the consequences (Poussard v Spiers; SGA 1979 ss 13-15)
Warranty: damages only (Bettini v Gye)
Innominate: depends on whether breach deprives of substantially whole benefit (Hongkong Fir)
Classification by statute, parties' express agreement (subject to Schuler v Wickman) or the courts
Commercial certainty can make time clauses conditions (Bunge v Tradax)
questions.modelAnswer: A condition is a term so important that any breach allows the innocent party to terminate and claim damages, regardless of consequences: in Poussard v Spiers (1876) a singer's absence from the opening nights was a breach of condition. Statute classifies some terms as conditions, e.g. Sale of Goods Act 1979 ss 13 to 15. A warranty is a lesser term; breach gives damages only, as in Bettini v Gye (1876), where missing rehearsals did not justify termination. An innominate term can be broken in serious or trivial ways, so the court looks at the effect: termination is allowed only if the breach deprives the innocent party of substantially the whole benefit (Hongkong Fir (1962)). Labels are not conclusive (Schuler v Wickman (1974)), but in commercial contracts time clauses are often treated as conditions for certainty (Bunge v Tradax (1981)).

questions.q: A mill's crankshaft breaks. The millers send it with carriers to engineers who will use it as a pattern for a new one, but the carriers delay delivery and the mill stays idle for longer. Treat the carriers as knowing only that they were carrying a broken mill shaft for millers. On Hadley v Baxendale, are the lost profits from the extra days of stoppage recoverable?
options: Yes, because all foreseeable losses are recoverable in contract
No, because lost profits can never be recovered in contract
No, because a stoppage was not the natural result of delay in carrying a shaft, and no special circumstances showing it would follow were known to the carriers
Yes, because lost profits always arise naturally from late delivery
questions.why: In Hadley the court held the loss fell outside limb one (a miller might well have a spare shaft, so a stoppage was not the natural consequence of delay) and outside limb two (the only circumstances the court treated as known to the carriers were that it was a broken shaft belonging to millers). Saying lost profits always arise naturally ignores that whether a loss is natural depends on the facts. 'All foreseeable losses' uses the wider tort test, which The Heron II rejected for contract. Lost profits are often recoverable (e.g. ordinary profits in Victoria Laundry), so 'never' is wrong.

questions.q: A builder installs a pool with a maximum depth of 6 ft 9 in (only 6 ft where people dive) instead of the agreed 7 ft 6 in. It is safe and the property's value is unaffected. Rebuilding would cost over £21,000. What did the House of Lords award in Ruxley v Forsyth?
options: Nothing, because there was no loss in market value
A modest award for loss of amenity, because rebuilding was out of all proportion to the benefit
An account of the builder's profits
The full cost of rebuilding, because the claimant is entitled to exactly what he contracted for
questions.why: The House of Lords restored the trial judge's award of £2,500 for loss of amenity (the Court of Appeal had awarded the cost of rebuilding). Full cost of cure was refused because it was unreasonable relative to the benefit. 'Nothing' ignores that the claimant lost something he valued (the consumer surplus) even though the market value did not change. An account of profits is the exceptional Blake remedy and was not in issue.

questions.q: Explain the two limbs of Hadley v Baxendale and how The Heron II refined the test. (5 marks)
markScheme: Limb one: losses arising naturally, in the usual course of things
Limb two: losses in reasonable contemplation of both parties at time of contracting, based on special knowledge
Victoria Laundry: ordinary profits recoverable, exceptional profits not without knowledge
Heron II: loss must be 'not unlikely'/serious possibility; stricter than tort's reasonable foreseeability
Type, not extent, of loss must be contemplated (Parsons v Uttley Ingham)
questions.modelAnswer: Hadley v Baxendale (1854) allows recovery for losses that arise naturally, in the usual course of things, from the breach (limb one), and for losses that both parties may reasonably be supposed to have contemplated, when they made the contract, as the probable result of breach (limb two). Limb two usually depends on special circumstances being communicated to the defendant. In Victoria Laundry (1949) ordinary lost profits were recoverable under limb one, but especially lucrative government contracts were too remote because the defendant did not know of them. The House of Lords in The Heron II (1969) held that contract requires a higher degree of probability than tort: the loss must have been 'not unlikely' or a serious possibility, not merely reasonably foreseeable. Parsons v Uttley Ingham (1978) adds that the type of loss, not its extent, must be within contemplation.

questions.q: A clause says a retail tenant 'shall keep the premises open for retail trade during usual hours'. The tenant closes because the shop loses money. The landlord seeks specific performance. Following Co-operative Insurance v Argyll, what will the court most likely do?
options: Refuse any remedy, because keep-open covenants are void
Order an account of the tenant's profits
Order the tenant to keep trading, because damages are always inadequate for breach of a lease
Refuse specific performance and leave the landlord to damages
questions.why: Co-op v Argyll refused to order a business to keep trading, mainly because it would need constant supervision and could cause the defendant losses out of proportion to the claimant's; damages were adequate. Saying damages are always inadequate in leases is wrong: land contracts are often specifically enforced, but an order to run a business is different. The covenant is valid, so the landlord can still claim damages. An account of profits is the exceptional Blake remedy and the closing tenant was making losses, not profits.

questions.q: Under Cavendish v Makdessi; ParkingEye v Beavis [2015] UKSC 67, what is the test for whether a clause is a penalty?
options: Whether the clause imposes a detriment out of all proportion to the innocent party's legitimate interest in enforcement of the primary obligation
Whether the sum is greater than the claimant's actual loss
Whether the clause was freely negotiated between parties of equal bargaining power
Whether the sum is a genuine pre-estimate of the loss likely to be caused by breach
questions.why: Makdessi replaced the narrow pre-estimate approach with the legitimate-interest test. The 'genuine pre-estimate' answer is the old Dunlop test, which the court said was too narrow for complex cases. 'Greater than actual loss' would make most fixed-sum clauses penalties, which is not the law. Equal bargaining power is a relevant factor (the court noted the parties in Makdessi were well advised), but it is not the test.

questions.q: Why did the House of Lords refuse specific performance in Co-operative Insurance Society v Argyll Stores [1998]? (5 marks)
markScheme: Settled practice not to order a party to carry on a business
Would require constant supervision / repeated applications to court
Enforcement by contempt is a heavy-handed and unsuitable weapon
Defendant could suffer loss far greater than claimant's (oppression / unjust enrichment of claimant)
Damages were an adequate remedy; distinction between orders to carry on an activity and to achieve a result
questions.modelAnswer: Argyll, the anchor tenant of a shopping centre, closed its supermarket in breach of a keep-open covenant. The House of Lords refused specific performance. Lord Hoffmann relied on settled practice not to order a defendant to carry on a business. Such an order would need constant supervision, because disputes about how the business was run could lead to repeated applications to the court. The only enforcement tool is contempt of court, which is a heavy-handed weapon in a commercial setting. The order could make the defendant suffer losses far greater than those the claimant suffered from the breach, which would be oppressive. He distinguished orders to carry on an activity from orders to achieve a result, such as building works. Damages were an adequate remedy.

questions.q: Problem question. Aditi runs a catering company. In January she contracts with Ben, a builder, to refurbish her kitchen for £60,000, to be completed by 1 June. Aditi has a contract to cater a large wedding on 10 June, with a £20,000 cancellation fee payable by her if she cannot perform. In April Ben tells Aditi that he has underpriced the job and will not be able to finish on time unless she pays him another £8,000. Aditi, unable to find another builder at short notice, agrees. Ben finishes on 30 May. Aditi pays the £60,000 but refuses to pay the extra £8,000, saying she was 'over a barrel'. Separately, Aditi owes her supplier, Chen, £5,000 due on 1 March. Chen agrees by email to take £4,000 'in full settlement', which Aditi pays on 1 March. In July Chen demands the remaining £1,000. Advise Aditi. (25 marks)
markScheme: Ben: consideration for the £8,000 promise: Stilk v Myrick; Williams v Roffey practical benefit (avoiding cancellation fee, getting the work completed on time)
Roffey proviso: promise must not be obtained by economic duress; contrast facts with Roffey where promisor volunteered extra payment

Duress analysis (Times Travel elements): threatened breach (illegitimate, Atlas Express v Kafco); causation (Huyton); no reasonable alternative (unable to find another builder); good/bad faith and protest (DSND)
Remedy: variation voidable; Aditi has not paid and has protested, so affirmation is unlikely (contrast The Atlantic Baron)
Chen: Foakes v Beer / Pinnel's Case: part payment on due date no consideration; Re Selectmove refuses to apply Roffey to debts; MWB v Rock left the point open
Promissory estoppel: clear promise ('in full settlement'), reliance, inequitable to go back? (High Trees; D & C Builders v Rees if pressure)
Effect of estoppel: can extinguish for past instalments/discrete debt arguments; suspensory point; as a shield only (Combe v Combe) which suits Aditi as defendant
Clear conclusions with reasoned weighing
questions.modelAnswer:
Ben's claim for £8,000

Ben will argue that Aditi's promise is supported by consideration. Under Stilk v Myrick (1809), performing an existing contractual duty owed to the promisor is not consideration. But in Williams v Roffey (1991) the Court of Appeal held that a promise to pay more for the same work can be binding if the promisor gets a practical benefit and the promise was not obtained by economic duress or fraud. Here Aditi does get practical benefits: the work was finished on time and she avoided the £20,000 cancellation fee and the trouble of finding a new builder. On consideration alone, Ben's argument looks strong.

The decisive issue is duress, which is the limit Roffey itself set. In Roffey the main contractor volunteered the extra money. Here Ben demanded it and threatened not to finish on time. Applying the elements set out by Lord Burrows in Times Travel (2021), Aditi must show illegitimate pressure, causation and no reasonable alternative. A threat to break a contract is often illegitimate, especially when made to exploit the other party's vulnerability: in Atlas Express v Kafco (1989) a carrier's threat to stop deliveries unless paid more was duress. Ben's honest mistake in pricing might suggest good faith (a factor in DSND Subsea (2000)), but he chose to use the wedding deadline to secure more money rather than ask for help without a threat. On causation (Huyton (1999)), Aditi agreed only because of the threat. She had no reasonable alternative, because she could not find another builder at short notice and suing Ben later would not have saved the wedding contract.

If duress is shown, the variation is voidable. Aditi has refused payment and complained, so unlike the buyer in The Atlantic Baron (1979) she has not affirmed. She is likely to defeat Ben's claim, although a court might be more sympathetic if it found Ben acted in good faith and Aditi had other options.

Chen's claim for £1,000

Under Pinnel's Case and Foakes v Beer (1884), paying £4,000 on the due date is not consideration for releasing the remaining £1,000; nothing new was given. Aditi cannot rely on Roffey: Re Selectmove (1995) refused to extend practical benefit to part payment of debts. In MWB v Rock (2018) the Supreme Court did not decide whether Foakes should be reconsidered, so it still binds.

Aditi's better argument is promissory estoppel (High Trees (1947)). Chen made a clear and unequivocal promise to accept £4,000 'in full settlement', and Aditi relied on it by paying. Nothing suggests Aditi pressured Chen, so D & C Builders v Rees (1966) does not stop the defence. Aditi uses estoppel as a shield against Chen's claim, which Combe v Combe (1951) allows. Estoppel is often only suspensory, but where a one-off debt has been settled on the strength of the promise, a court may hold that it would be inequitable for Chen to reclaim the balance. Aditi has a reasonable defence, but the law is uncertain.

questions.q: Essay. 'English contract law claims to protect the claimant's expectation interest, but its remedial rules regularly leave the promisee with less than performance.' Discuss with reference to damages and specific remedies. (25 marks)
markScheme: Starting point: expectation measure (Robinson v Harman); specific performance secondary and discretionary
Limits on damages: remoteness (Hadley; Heron II; The Achilleas), mitigation (British Westinghouse), non-pecuniary loss rule (Addis; exceptions Farley)
Ruxley: cost of cure versus difference in value; consumer surplus recognised only in part
Specific performance refused where damages adequate and for business operation (Co-op v Argyll); personal services
Agreed sums and White and Carter (legitimate interest) show some protection of performance; penalties (Makdessi) protect legitimate interest in performance
Gain-based awards: AG v Blake (exceptional), One Step negotiating damages limited
Evaluation: efficient breach and cost arguments versus performance interest (e.g. Friedmann, Webb); course theme of social consequences
Reasoned conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
The starting point supports the claim. Robinson v Harman (1848) states that damages aim to put the claimant in the position as if the contract had been performed. But that is protection of the value of performance in money, not of performance itself, and several rules reduce even that.

First, limits on damages. Losses that are too remote are excluded: in Hadley v Baxendale (1854) the mill owners' lost profits were not recoverable, and The Heron II (1969) requires loss to be 'not unlikely'. The Achilleas (2008) went further by asking whether the defendant assumed responsibility for the type of loss. The mitigation rule (British Westinghouse (1912)) puts the cost of avoidable loss on the claimant. Disappointment is generally not compensated (Addis (1909)), though Farley v Skinner (2001) recognises exceptions where peace of mind or pleasure was an important object. Each rule cuts recovery below full performance value.

Second, Ruxley v Forsyth (1996) shows the gap clearly. Mr Forsyth contracted for a 7 ft 6 in pool and did not get it. The cost of cure was refused as out of all proportion to the benefit. The £2,500 loss of amenity award recognised his 'consumer surplus', but he did not get what he paid for.

Third, specific relief is secondary. Specific performance is discretionary and depends on damages being inadequate. In Co-op v Argyll (1998) the House of Lords refused to make Argyll keep its store open, citing supervision, the bluntness of contempt and disproportionate loss to the defendant. Contracts for personal services are generally not specifically enforced. In practice a defendant can often pay damages instead of performing.

Some rules point the other way. The action for an agreed sum is not subject to remoteness or mitigation, and White and Carter (1962) allowed a party to perform and claim the price, subject to the legitimate interest limit. Makdessi (2015) recognises a legitimate interest in performance beyond compensation, which can support agreed sums. AG v Blake (2001) allowed an account of profits where the claimant had a legitimate interest in preventing profit-making, and One Step (2018) allows negotiating damages where a valuable right such as a restrictive covenant is lost. But Blake is expressly exceptional and One Step narrowed negotiating damages.

Evaluation: the law protects performance through money, accepting that sometimes a promisee will get less than performance. Supporters argue that this avoids waste (Ruxley, Argyll) and fits commercial expectations. Critics argue that it undervalues non-financial interests and lets promisors break deliberately. Since LL142 asks whether doctrines are justified by their social effects, a strong answer will weigh efficiency against fairness to consumers and weaker parties. The statement is broadly accurate: English law protects the expected value of performance but, through remoteness, mitigation, Ruxley and the discretion over specific performance, often leaves the promisee with less than full performance.
